Row.Text: The first flowerings of a recognizable Japan emerge with the introduction of Buddhism and the Chinese script in 538 CE. But it is the Heian era (794-1185 CE) where recognizably Japanese arts and literature shine. From the meticulously laid-out city of Heian-kyo (present-day Kyoto) grew an era of relative calm, so much so that its very name – Heian – means “peace.” The capital was a place of poetry, of refinement, of courtly life and intrigue.

But the vantage point from Heian’s palaces and street grids is a limited one. Outside of the city walls, conflict ran through the Heian countryside, both between the Japanese-speaking population and the remnants of the Jomon people in the north, as well as between rural lords dealing with widespread poverty and banditry and a central court wrapped up in its own cultural production.

Prior to Heian, Japan had deep cultural links with China, seeing the Chinese Tang Dynasty as a source of Buddhist knowledge and literary culture. But as Tang faced growing instability and eventual collapse in 907 CE, these links were severed and Heian, left on its own, moved forward its own cultural and religious innovations.

And it flourished: while writing using Chinese characters and in Chinese language had been practiced among the elite of Japan for some centuries prior, the writers of Heian took their own path, especially in the culture of the court women. New writing systems – katakana and hiragana – were developed to better capture Japanese language, and in the 11th century, the writer Murasaki Shikibu composed The Tale of Genji, a dramatic account of court romance that is widely considered the first novel.

Heian was also marked by elaborations upon Buddhist life, a cosmopolitan religion that coexisted with the indigenous Shinto practice. In the rarefied realm of the Heian court, the elaborate rituals of Tendai and Shingon Buddhism were in vogue, whereas in the countryside the simplified “pure land” Amida Buddhism gained sway. These cultural splits between nobility and commoners furthered the isolation – the splendid isolation – of the court, even as lawlessness and economic crisis threatened the land.

Outside of Heian-kyo, the lords of the shoen, the rural manor, found the need to create a class of soldiers and knights in order to maintain control in the face of widespread banditry. These were the samurai, and as their martial power grew, they were to make their mark upon Japanese politics in the years to come.

Out of conflict between the refined city and martial country, powerful clans arose. The most influential of these was the Heian-kyo (Kyoto)-based Fujiwara. Fujiwara was deeply entwined with the central court, as lords sent their daughters to the imperial palace and exerted a strong influence upon the emperors that emerged from this line. But this system of informal control was to break: Emperor Go-Sanjo, one of the first emperors in centuries to not have a Fujiwara mother, made it his mission to purge the Fujiwara from their positions of influence. The Fujiwara made a last, desperate bid for power in the Hogen Rebellion of 1156 CE, but were crushed. But if Go-Sanjo sought independence, he did not find it: out of this war came not a new period of direct imperial control free from clan influence, but a substitution of Fujiwara puppet masters for another clan, the Taira.

Taira machinations were also to end in tragedy as other clans, seeing the fall of Fujiwara, sought to try their hand – notably, in the Genpei War between the Kyoto-based Taira and the rising Minamoto clan, whose power base was in the countryside. In the Battle of Dan-no-ura, on the Shimonoseki Strait in 1185 CE, the Taira fleet was destroyed. According to legend, the Taira families, watching the battle from the shores, flung themselves into the sea rather than face defeat. The victorious Minamoto were to relocate the base of practical power to Kamakura, though the court and capital remained Kyoto. This configuration – a distant military capital protecting an inward-looking court – created a new era of power and a new model of rule: the shogunate.

Originally built as a manor for a Minamoto lord in 998 CE, Byodo-in became a temple under the Fujiwara clan in 1052 CE. In the year following, the temple constructed a dramatic hall, with sweeping outstretched wings enfolding an artificial lake. The structure resembled a phoenix – hoo, in Japanese – and the hall is now known as “Hoo-do,” or the Phoenix Hall. Gracing its top is a golden statue of the hoo, gazing down upon the majesty of the place.

The hall was designed as a home for Amida or Pure Land Buddhism, a more populist style of Buddhism that emphasized a yearning for rebirth. This yearning was telling – Amida followers believed that the final age of Buddhism was nigh, and that through devotion and the repetition of the name of the Pure Land, “Amida,” one could gain life there, after the present world had declined. An image of the Amida Buddha in gilded cypress wood was installed in the hall.
The world has yet to end, but the hall and the Buddha image remain.

Religion in Japan can be, for outsiders, a complicated affair, with Shinto shrines, Buddhist temples, and references to Confucianism all situated within the realm of what is today a relatively secular society. But the jinja or Shinto shrine is still a powerful symbol of the indigenous religion of the Japanese isles, one that places the kami – gods both large and small – at its center. The kami are housed and venerated at these shrines, where they receive requests for luck, fortune, or to remove (and sometimes deliver) misfortune or a curse. Jinja also fill roles in society that the more transcendental Buddhism does not take up – marriage, for instance, is traditionally a Shinto ritual, interested as it is in the propagation of earthly matters, whereas death and its link to the beyond falls under the realm of Buddhism. These shrines are often located in places of natural beauty, where kami dwell in mountains or waterfalls, or, occasionally, at the seaside.

Shinto in the Heian era was firmly established as a key faith – a Heian-era text, the Engi-shiki, lists the over two thousand shrines of the land (and the over three thousand kami worshipped in them). The Engi-shiki, too, listed the ways that one might appeal to the kami, as securing the favor of various kami could be a means to success in war, business, or the simple uncertainty of life in ancient Japan.

More properly the Ritsuryo-sei, this code based on Chinese law structured early Japanese society. Elites in the Asuka and Nara periods, just preceding Heian, drew upon a wealth of knowledge borrowed from Tang China that they used – with varying success – to forge unity on what was a fractured Japan. Ritsuryo centralized power in the court and established official ministries in charge of various aspects of Japanese society. Additionally, it standardized rules of conduct, crime, and taxation, and imposed a separation of social classes. As with many such imports from China, as Heian cut ties with Tang and progressed down its own, uniquely Japanese, path, the Ritsuryo system declined in importance during the Heian period.

As Heian’s ties with Tang China declined, Japanese writers created their own literary styles, including (arguably) the creation of the novel, the invention of kana (phonetic characters), and the development of waka – Japanese poetry. The term is broad, simply referring to Japanese literature and encompassing the better-known haiku, but in Heian times waka most often took the form of the tanka, a slightly longer poem than haiku. While waka poets could be men (Ki no Tsurayuki, for instance), women such as Izumi Shikibu and Murasaki Shikibu (author of the Tale of Genji) wrote a significant portion of Heian literature, especially works composed in kana. While the haiku form of waka came to predominate in later periods, waka continues to be written today.

Heian-kyo – modern-day Kyoto – was to be a model for a new Japan. Built by the Emperor Kammu in 794 CE, Heian-kyo was modeled after the Tang capital at Chang’an, and like that city, was built on an urban grid. This grid was not just aesthetically pleasing; it was a model for society. The palace sat at the northern end of the city and the rest was divided into boulevards separating areas for commerce, administration, residence, and urban villas. The city also followed the principles of geomancy – a properly-laid-out town would ensure prosperity for the state. Yet the grid proved too ambitious: the outskirts of the capital had gone to farmland by the end of the period.

Everything that we see, and that we are, is transient. Flowers bloom, shrivel, and fall. Youth ages and even the noblest of us die. But such transient things are full of emotion on account of their temporary nature; the knowledge that a moment is transient contains within it a wistfulness that makes it all the more beautiful while it lives. This acknowledgement of the beauty of impermanence – what in Buddhism is termed anicca – was a core feature of Heian literature and remains a key principle in understanding Japanese aesthetics.

For much of early Japanese history, Japanese authors wrote and read Chinese poetry – works by poets such as Li Bai were considered masterpieces in Heian, as they are today. But as Heian Japan grew and Tang China declined, this inspiration turned inward, and in the 800s, the Japanese ambassador to China, Sugawara Michizane, declined his post, claiming that China had nothing more to give.

What emerged from the following isolation was a flowering of literature. Japanese writing began to incorporate the phonetic kana (hiragana and katakana) that enabled expression in Japanese language. Writing styles focused on melancholic themes – love and love’s ending, the fading of summer into autumn, or the appeal of ruins – and took inspiration from the image of the cloud-shrouded moon. “Poem tales,” novelistic works of prose, became particularly popular, especially among female writers, and Murasaki Shikibu’s Tale of Genji, written around 1010 CE, ranks supreme among these: a tale of an imperial son of a low-ranking concubine who, stripped of his position, spends his time in love affairs amidst the splendor of a court whose highest levels have been denied him.

A term for a weapon, not a person, yumi refers to the Japanese bow. Along with the iconic sword (in Heian’s time, the heavier tachi), the bow was one of the significant weapons of the samurai class. A yumi is smaller on the bottom, but extends upwards in a large arc. Its massive frame meant power, and its asymmetry meant that it could be used on horseback or kneeling. During Heian, bowyers experimented with fusing wood and bamboo to further increase the projectile power of the bow, making an already deadly weapon more devastating.

The most famous Japanese archer of the time was Nasu no Yoichi, a samurai of the Minamoto clan who allegedly shot the Taira banner from their flagship in one shot, demonstrating the superiority of the Minamoto forces in the conflicts between the clans.
